scenes.say: A hundred downloads, a second each. One way takes a hundred seconds. Another takes one. Which tool? By the end you'll know, and spot the Python bugs.
Today you'll do three things. Pick a process, a thread, or async for the job. Explain the GIL, races and deadlocks. And dodge the classic Python traps.

scenes.title: Process, thread, or async?
scenes.statement: Three ways to do many things at once. Say what each one shares, and what each one costs.

example.output: about 1 s, with the right tool

scenes.say: Here's the problem. Three ways to do many things at once. For example, a hundred downloads, a second each. The answer: about one second, with the right tool. Interviewers ask this first.

scenes.head: The puzzle we'll solve
scenes.say: Here's where we're heading. Downloads one by one: a hundred seconds. A pool of ten threads: about ten. Asyncio: about one. Then the twist. The same threads on number crunching: no faster at all.

scenes.head: A restaurant, three ways
scenes.say: Think of a restaurant. A process is a separate restaurant, with its own kitchen and fridge. Threads are cooks sharing one kitchen and one fridge: fast, but they can collide. Async is one waiter with many tables. He takes an order and moves on.

scenes.head: What does each one share?
scenes.say: Now the real thing. One process owns its memory. Inside it, threads are separate lines of execution. Each has its own stack, but all share the heap. Sharing is cheap, and that causes race conditions. A second process has completely separate memory. Safer, but talking across is slower.
Your turn. A global x is zero. A worker sets it to ninety nine, once as a thread, once as a process. Main prints x. What do you see?
scenes.q: Worker sets x = 99. Main prints x. Thread vs process?

scenes.head: Same global, two answers
scenes.say: A thread shares the heap, so main sees ninety nine. A process got its own copy of memory, so main still sees zero. Same line, different memory. That answers what each shares.

panels.code:
def run(kind):
    global x
    x = 0
    w = kind(target=bump)
    w.start(); w.join()
    print(kind.__name__, x)

run(Thread)
run(Process)

setup.app.py:
from threading import Thread
import multiprocessing as mp
from multiprocessing import Process
mp.set_start_method("fork")

def bump():
    global x
    x = 99

scenes.title: Make 100 downloads take 1 s
scenes.statement: A scraper fetches 100 URLs, one at a time. Make it fast without adding CPU.
scenes.note: Time is spent waiting, not computing
scenes.say: Here's the problem. A scraper fetches URLs one at a time. For example, a hundred URLs, a second each. We want one second, not a hundred. The time is spent waiting.

scenes.head: The slow scraper
scenes.say: A new hire writes a scraper. A for loop, one URL at a time. A hundred pages, a second each: a hundred seconds. The CPU isn't busy. It's waiting on the network. And waiting is the part we can overlap.

scenes.head: A pool of ten threads
scenes.say: A thread pool keeps ten workers. Each fetch sleeps one second. Ten run at once, so a hundred downloads take ten rounds. About ten seconds. While one thread waits, the others run.

panels.code:
from concurrent.futures import (
    ThreadPoolExecutor)

with ThreadPoolExecutor(10) as pool:
    list(pool.map(fetch, urls))

scenes.say: Predict. Same hundred downloads, one second each, but now twenty workers instead of ten. How long does it take?
scenes.q: 100 downloads, 1 s each, 20 threads. Total time?

scenes.head: More workers, fewer rounds
scenes.say: Total time. One worker takes a hundred. Ten workers take ten. Twenty take five, since a hundred over twenty is five rounds. But asyncio does it in about one second, with no extra threads.

scenes.head: Async: one thread, 100 tasks
scenes.say: That's our answer to the problem. At await, the function says: I'm waiting, run something else. Gather starts all hundred together. Every sleep overlaps, so the whole thing takes about a second, on a single thread.

panels.code:
async def afetch(url):
    await asyncio.sleep(1)
async def main():
    await asyncio.gather(
        *(afetch(u) for u in urls))
t = time.perf_counter()
asyncio.run(main())
print(round(time.perf_counter() - t), "s")

setup.app.py:
import asyncio, time
urls = [f"page{i}" for i in range(100)]

scenes.head: The event loop
scenes.say: Who runs this? The event loop: one thread with a queue of tasks. Task A runs until it hits an await. The loop parks it, and runs task B. When A's reply arrives, the loop resumes A. It is cooperative: tasks take turns by choice.

scenes.head: One blocking call ruins it
scenes.say: The mistake: calling async multithreading. It's one thread. So a task that never awaits blocks everyone. Both of these run two tasks. The good one awaits sleep. The bad one calls time sleep, and the tasks queue up. Async wins, if nothing blocks.

panels.code:
async def good():
    await asyncio.sleep(1)

async def bad():
    time.sleep(1)   # never awaits

setup.run.py:
import asyncio, time
from app import good, bad

async def run(fn):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    await asyncio.gather(fn(), fn())
    print(fn.__name__, round(time.perf_counter() - t), "s")

asyncio.run(run(good))
asyncio.run(run(bad))

scenes.title: Why are threads no faster?
scenes.statement: Four CPU-heavy jobs on four threads take as long as one by one. Why, and what works?
scenes.say: Here's the problem. Four jobs that crunch numbers, run on four threads. For example, one million squares each. It takes as long as one by one. Why, and what works?

scenes.head: The GIL: one microphone
scenes.say: Standard Python has a rule: the G I L, the global interpreter lock. Picture one microphone. Only one thread may run Python code at a time. A thread waiting on the network hands the mic over. Number crunching never waits, so threads just take turns.

scenes.head: Four CPU-heavy jobs
scenes.say: Test it. Four jobs, each crunching one million squares. One by one takes about two seconds. Four threads: no faster, they just share the mic. Four processes each get their own interpreter, and finish much sooner.

output.text:
sequential 1.8 s
threads 2.2 s
processes 1.0 s

scenes.say: Your turn. Two jobs. Resize five hundred photos on an eight core laptop, pure crunching. Then download five hundred more photos. Which tool for each?
scenes.q: Resize 500 photos, then download 500. Best tool for each?

scenes.head: Which one do I pick?
scenes.say: Processes, then async. Pure crunching needs real parallel cores, and each process has its own GIL. Waiting on network or disk? Async or threads: cheap, thousands can wait. Need separate memory for safety? Processes again. That's why threads failed.

scenes.title: Why does the counter come up short?
scenes.statement: Two threads each add one to a shared counter, 100,000 times. The total should be 200,000.
scenes.say: Here's the problem. Two threads share one counter. For example, each adds one, a hundred thousand times. We need exactly two hundred thousand, every run. Shared memory is the catch.

scenes.head: A race condition
scenes.say: Even with the GIL, shared data breaks. The counter is five. Thread one reads five. Thread two reads five, before one writes. Both write six. Two adds, but the counter moved once. The result depends on timing. That's a race condition.

scenes.head: The fix: a lock
scenes.say: That's our answer to the problem: a lock. With lock means only one thread is inside that block at a time. Two threads each add a hundred thousand times, and every run gives exactly two hundred thousand. The other fix is to avoid shared state.
One more bug. Thread one holds lock A and waits for lock B. Thread two holds lock B and waits for lock A. What happens?
scenes.q: T1 holds A, wants B. T2 holds B, wants A. Result?

scenes.head: Deadlock
scenes.say: Deadlock. Each thread waits for the lock the other one holds, so neither ever moves. No error, the program just hangs. The fix: take the locks in the same order. Locks fix the counter, and order avoids deadlock.

scenes.title: Spot the Python gotchas
scenes.statement: Snippets that look right but print surprises. Predict each one before you run it.
scenes.say: Here's the problem. Code that looks right and lies. For example, a function with an empty list default, called twice. You expect one, then two. Watch what happens.

scenes.head: A name is a sticky note
scenes.say: Python variables are sticky notes, not boxes. A is a note on the list. B is a second note on the same list, not a new one. Copy makes a real second list. Append through B, and A sees three. C is unchanged.

panels.code:
a = [1, 2]
b = a
c = a.copy()
b.append(3)
print(a)  # [1, 2, 3]
print(c)  # [1, 2]

scenes.head: The mutable default
scenes.say: Same idea, hidden in a default. That empty list is built once, when the function is defined. Every call shares it. So the second call sees the first call's item. The fix: None, then build inside.

panels.code:
def add(x, items=[]):
    items.append(x)
    return items

print(add(1))
print(add(2))

scenes.say: Predict. Three lambdas built in a loop, each returning i. We call each one. What list do we get?
scenes.q:
fs = [lambda: i for i in range(3)]
[f() for f in fs]  gives?

scenes.head: Late binding
scenes.say: Two, two, two. A lambda looks up i when it is called, not when it is made. By then the loop ended and i is two. Fix it by freezing the value as a default argument: i equals i. Now zero, one, two.

panels.code:
fs = [lambda: i for i in range(3)]
print([f() for f in fs])

gs = [lambda i=i: i for i in range(3)]
print([f() for f in gs])

scenes.head: is versus ==
scenes.say: One more. Equals asks: same value? Is asks: same object? Two separate lists with the same items are equal, but not the same object. Use is for None, equals for the rest. That answers it.

scenes.title: A million squares, little memory
scenes.statement: Sum a million squares without holding them all, and wrap a function without losing its name.
scenes.say: Here's the problem. Add up a million squares. For example, i times i, for i under a million. We want it in tiny memory. Then wrap a function, and keep its name.

scenes.head: Generators are lazy
scenes.say: A generator uses yield. Yield pauses the function and hands back one value. Next resumes it. The first next gives zero. The second gives one. Nothing is computed early.

scenes.head: A million squares: bytes
scenes.say: Here we compare memory, with get size of. The list of a million squares: over eight million bytes. The generator for the same million: two hundred eight.

scenes.head: Decorators wrap functions
scenes.say: A decorator is a function that takes a function and returns a new one. The wrapper runs extra code around the call. Writing at logged above work means work becomes logged of work. And functools wraps keeps the original name.
Last prediction. Delete the functools wraps line. We print work dot dunder name. What does it print?

scenes.head: Why people forget wraps
scenes.say: Wrapper. Without wraps, it wears the wrapper's name. That breaks debuggers. With wraps, it stays work. That answers it.

scenes.head: Say it in 25 seconds
scenes.say: Process, thread, async? Own memory, shared memory, one thread. Race condition? Timing decides the result, so I use a lock. GIL? One thread runs Python at a time. Deadlock? Two threads wait on each other. Pick? Async for waiting, processes for crunching.
rows: Timing decides; I use a lock.
One thread runs Python at a time.
Two threads wait on each other.
Async to wait, processes to crunch.

scenes.head: Python gotchas, aloud
scenes.say: Assignment never copies, names share objects. A default list is built once, so I default to None. The GIL hurts threads on crunching but not waiting, so processes for crunching. A generator makes values on demand. A decorator wraps a function.

scenes.head: Try these this week
scenes.say: Three exercises. Time your own slow loop with a thread pool, then asyncio. Break a counter without a lock, then fix it. Write a decorator and delete wraps to see the damage.
rows: Two threads, shared counter, no lock

scenes.say: So say this. A process has its own memory, threads share it, async yields at await. Waiting work: async or threads. Crunching: processes, because of the GIL. And watch defaults, late binding, and assignment that never copies.
lines: Process: own memory. Thread: shared. Async: yields.
Waiting: async or threads. CPU: processes.
Defaults run once; assignment never copies.
